messages.author: 37abdbe6ce54889a
messages.subject: BYM model precision
parts:
Dear Dr.Rue and Experts:

I've recently notice that in R-INLA:

If I specified a "bym" for random effect in an identity link, I get three precision parameters:
Precision for the Gaussian observations
Precision for fips (iid component)      
Precision for fips (spatial component)    


Should BYM model have only two component ? One is structured and another is unstructured ?



Thanks,
Xiao

> Precision for fips (iid component)

its usually only two hyperparameters since the responce is poisson, but
with gaussian responce, you get one more.

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] BYM model precision
parts:
On Thu, 2016-02-11 at 08:53 -0800, Xiao Li wrote:
> Thanks Dr.Rue, so in Gaussian case, is it redundant to specify 'iid',
> since the error is is also an 'iid', although not the same
> precision..

that is somewhat true. if you have replicates, then you have sum of two
terms, one that is common over all replicates, and one that might vary
over replicates. so there is some structure you can explore. if the
responce has the same variances for all, then, yes, replace model="bym"
with model="besag", and you're done. 
--
Håvard Rue
he...@r-inla.org

parts:
It's unclear to me what your model is. If it's a replicated model where the non-replicated model has 36 latent variables, the replicated model does _not_ have 127 copies of the outcomes of the model; it has 127 _different_ outcomes of the model. I may have misunderstood what you're trying to achieve, as I haven't fully followed the whole thread, sorry.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] BYM model precision
parts:
One possibility is to add an unobserved individual, as 128th replicate. With NA as observation for it, you get a model that tries to predict a new individual, which seems to be what you want?  Then the sampler should give you the right thing (I.e. Posterior samples for the observed individual, and a sample from the estimated model for the 128th) I believe.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] BYM model precision
parts:
Dr.Lindgren,

Sorry for the confusion, I will think about it more carefully, and updated this thread sometime later 

Thanks a lot for the help !

Xiao

On Sun, Feb 14, 2016 at 1:20 PM, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:

Now given a y_new vector with 36 outcomes, I want to compute the p(y_new | all y,hypers,fixed effect) = (1/M)*sum_{1:M} p(y_new | eta(36*1 dimension), hypers, all y,fixed effect), where eta are drew from posterior p(eta| all y,hypers) .

This is not a complete and self-consistent statement. For starters, there are clearly lots of missing indices here.

Finn

where in the right hand side of equation p(y_new | eta(36*1 dimension), hypers, all y,fixed effect) is normal distribution.

The question is how can I obtain draws from posterior p(eta| all y,hypers), can I use the first 36 of the big latent vector of the full model from inla.posterior.sample() 


Xiao







On Sun, Feb 14, 2016 at 12:43 PM, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
But you have 36 new latent variables for that individual as well, correct?
Your probability statement just says "latent" in the conditioning, but it's then not clear which latent variables you want to condition on, and which ones you want to marginalized over. You'll probably need to explicitly write down the whole model, with complete notation for all variables, so that it's clear precisely what the model is, and precisely what it is that you should compute.

Finn

On 14 Feb 2016, at 18:27, Xiao Li <lixiao...@gmail.com> wrote:

Dr.Lindgren, so in this case, can I use the first 36 realization of the the full latent vector which is 36*127 of the full model ? or the average of the 36 latent variables ?

Thanks a lot !

Xiao

On Sun, Feb 14, 2016 at 12:23 PM, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
Ok, that's a bit different, yes. Sorry for the confusion.

Finn

On 14 Feb 2016, at 18:16, Xiao Li <lixiao...@gmail.com> wrote:

Dr.Lindgren, Thanks for helping on this.

I'm not predicting a subject, initially I have 2 sets of groups,say, each group have 100 subjects and each subject have 36 outcomes.  
I fitted them separately, so I get different parameters for the two groups.

Then I transferred to classification framework, which requires to obtain the predictive posterior density , so I need to draw the latent first, and then calculate p( ynew | y,latent, hypers )


Xiao

On Sun, Feb 14, 2016 at 12:06 PM, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
One possibility is to add an unobserved individual, as 128th replicate. With NA as observation for it, you get a model that tries to predict a new individual, which seems to be what you want?  Then the sampler should give you the right thing (I.e. Posterior samples for the observed individual, and a sample from the estimated model for the 128th) I believe.

Finn

On 14 Feb 2016, at 17:56, Xiao Li <lixiao...@gmail.com> wrote:

Dr.Lindgren,

Let me briefly introduce some background: 

For a single outcome subject(Y), I have 36 outcomes and these 36 outcomes are spatially correlated. 
Now I have 127 subjects, with each subject(Y) has a 36 coutcome. 

I used the replication statement as these 127 subjects are from the same group, share the same hypers , but these 127 people are iid.  

Now given a new subject, I want to compute p( ynew | y,latent, hypers ), I have difficult in use the posterior sample to get one realization of the 36*1 latent variables...


Xiao

On Sun, Feb 14, 2016 at 11:47 AM, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
It's unclear to me what your model is. If it's a replicated model where the non-replicated model has 36 latent variables, the replicated model does _not_ have 127 copies of the outcomes of the model; it has 127 _different_ outcomes of the model. I may have misunderstood what you're trying to achieve, as I haven't fully followed the whole thread, sorry.

Finn

On 14 Feb 2016, at 17:40, Xiao Li <lixiao...@gmail.com> wrote:

Thanks Dr.Lindgren, 

Now I have a single Y (with 36 outcome corresponds to the 36 latent variables), I want to compute the predictive density for this new Y, 
I want to use draw the latent, and use that realization to compute the  p( ynew | y,latent, hypers ), can I use the first 36 latent or average of 36 latents,since the 127 copies are from the same latent population ?

Xiao

On Sunday, February 14, 2016 at 10:40:38 AM UTC-6, Finn Lindgren wrote:
If your model has 127 replications of a model with 36 latent variables, that means that the full model has 36*127 latent variables. This is part of what replicating a model means.

Finn

On 14 Feb 2016, at 16:15, Xiao Li <lixiao...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Dr.Rue and Dear , 

It is still about the replication problem.
I tried to use the inla.posterior.sample() to get posterior sample to do further calculation, I need to draw values from the marginal posterior probability of the latent variables, as well as hypers,
and then substitute these values to calculate the predictive density p( ynew | y,latent, hypers ).

But what I get is a 4572(=36*127)X1 dimension vector of the latent. I thought since it is a model with replications, so the actual latent variable is actually 36X1 dimension, so my question is How can I get 36X1 vector of the latents ?
Are these 127 copies of latent independent ? If so, can I use just one copy to substitute ?
 

Many Thanks in advance !


Xiao

On Thu, Feb 11, 2016 at 10:56 AM, INLA help <he...@r-inla.org> wrote:
On Thu, 2016-02-11 at 08:53 -0800, Xiao Li wrote:
> Thanks Dr.Rue, so in Gaussian case, is it redundant to specify 'iid',
> since the error is is also an 'iid', although not the same
> precision..

that is somewhat true. if you have replicates, then you have sum of two
terms, one that is common over all replicates, and one that might vary
over replicates. so there is some structure you can explore. if the
responce has the same variances for all, then, yes, replace model="bym"
with model="besag", and you're done. 
--
Håvard Rue
he...@r-inla.org
